title: Molinists against Jansenius: grace in the will's power
source_text: IX. Verum quanquam hac in parte Jansenius multos sectatores habeat, eos nempe qui singulari modo se discipulos Augustini vocant, haec tamen illius doctrina rejicitur a maxima Scholae Romanae parte: eique palam repugnant, tam qui Molinae Jesuitae Methodum & doctrinam sequuntur, quam qui recentiores Thomistae appellantur. Nam priores illi volunt gratiam Christi, non minus quam gratiam primo homini nondum lapso collatam, sic in potestate voluntatis esse, ut pro innata libertate, illa uti, vel non uti possit, & reipsa saepe non utatur: adeoque a libero arbitrio pendere, ut gratia Christi sit efficax, vel non efficax; & effectum suum in hominis conversione obtineat, vel non obtineat.
pass_a_gloss: IX. But although in this part Jansenius has many followers, those namely who in a singular manner call themselves disciples of Augustine, yet this doctrine of his is rejected by the greatest part of the Roman School: and to it openly are opposed, both those who follow the Method and doctrine of Molina the Jesuit, and those who are called the more recent Thomists. For those former will that the grace of Christ, not less than the grace conferred on the first man not yet fallen, is so in the power of the will, that according to innate liberty, it can use it, or not use it, and in fact often does not use it: and so depends on free choice, that the grace of Christ is efficacious, or not efficacious; and obtains its effect in the conversion of man, or does not obtain it.
pass_b_english: Thesis IX. On this point Jansenius has many followers, namely those who call themselves disciples of Augustine in a special sense. Even so, this teaching of his is rejected by most of the Roman School. Both the followers of the method and teaching of Molina the Jesuit and those called the recent Thomists openly oppose it.

The first group hold that the grace of Christ, no less than the grace given to the first man before he fell, is in the will's power in such a way that, by its inborn liberty, the will can use it or not use it, and in fact often does not.
So, on their view, it depends on free choice whether Christ's grace is efficacious or not, and whether it achieves its effect in a man's conversion or fails to.
